newsitem.title: USA: U.S. manufacturers struggle to meet demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. manufacturers struggle to meet demand.

text.p: Manufacturing activity gained steam in February as businesses struggled to keep pace with free-spending consumers, industry and government reports released on Monday showed.
The National Association of Purchasing Management said its closely watched index rose to 53.1 from 52 in January, with any reading over 50 denoting an accelerating pace of business.
Analysts said busier rates of production, rising orders and longer delivery times indicated businesses were responding to more buying by consumers and were trying to build inventories.
Separately, the Commerce Department reported that January consumer spending increased briskly, by 0.7 percent, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.3 trillion.
It was the strongest surge in consumer spending since last October, when it grew by 0.9 percent and followed a slim 0.2 percent December gain.
Personal incomes from wages, salaries and other sources like rents and bank interest rose a more modest 0.3 percent in January to a rate of $6.65 trillion after a 0.7 percent December rise.
Brisk consumer spending at the start of 1997 was putting some pressure on industry.

"Manufacturing industries clearly are trying to crank out as many pieces as they can both to meet demand and to replenish inventories," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis, adding that it was likely to add to Federal Reserve policy-makers' concern about inflation.

"The boom in the manufacturing sector is putting pressure on prices and also on delivery times," Sohn said, noting that the NAPM index also showed a decline in employment that likely was related to tight labour markets.
"There just aren't enough bodies to be hired in many industries and so some people are resorting to bounties to get the staff they need," Sohn added.
The purchasing managers, whose survey is closely watched since these executives buy vital materials that factories use, said that 13 industries reported paying higher prices in February.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan strongly hinted last Wednesday that the central bank may need to raise interest rates in coming months to contain inflation. His remarks to Congress sent a ripple of unease through financial markets that continues, with Greenspan scheduled to testify again on Wednesday.
The Fed chief said monetary policy might need to be tightened before evidence of price pressures emerges.
"The reports today are an important piece of evidence to support Chairman Greenspan's threat last week that all good things come to an end and that we might see higher inflation ahead," Sohn said.

In a third report issued on Monday, the Commerce Department said spending on new construction edged up in January by 0.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $589.8 billion after a 0.9 percent drop in December.

The slight recovery in January building partly reflected a bounceback from exceptionally bad weather in December, notably in the West, where storms and flooding stymied homebuilding and other construction.

But most significantly, it also showed a 2.9 percent pickup in spending on privately financed projects like offices and industrial parks that analysts said reflected businesses' need for more warehousing and manufacturing capacity.
By contrast, spending on new homes and apartments barely gained, up 0.4 percent from December, as this sector showed signs of leveling off.
The NAPM index showed a significant pickup in prices during February and a kick upward in delivery times, which means that factories were so busy it took them longer to fill orders.

While some analysts said runups in commodities like oil and natural gas have eased in recent weeks, they said there was cause for concern that rising prices and longer lead times to meet demand pointed to "a deterioration in benign inflation.

"They're not gruesome, but as Greenspan alluded to last Wednesday, they certainly would bear close watching and the trend is not a favourable trend right now," said Joseph Liro, an economist with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities in New York.
